solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: About to have a bonk? Earthy stuff!

blocks.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
a lay is a bout of sex, as is a bonk

explanation.surface: Someone is on the point of a quick romp and the setter cheers at its earthiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonk' is British slang for sex; LAY is its slang equivalent. 'Earthy' suggests crude talk but means literally of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Clay is a fine-grained soil, so it is literally material dug from the ground.

clue.text: It might give a Cyclopean view of our magazine cover

definitions.text: It might give a Cyclopean view

blocks.note: this puzzle runs in Private Eye, often called just the Eye
a patch is a piece of material covering something

explanation.surface: A one-eyed giant's-eye view of the front of this very magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appears in Private Eye, a British satirical magazine, so 'our magazine' is EYE. 'Cover' looks like the front page but is the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad worn over one socket leaves its wearer with single-sided vision, like the mythical one-eyed giant.

clue.text: Labour needs a name for a political catchphrase

blocks.note: a slog is hard work, labour
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: The Labour Party is told it needs a snappy name to campaign under.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital-L 'Labour' looks like the party, but it is plain toil.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan is a short memorable phrase used by a party or campaign to rally support.

clue.text: Virgin, so make out to a smaller extent

blocks.note: to make out something is to discern or spot it
less means to a smaller degree

explanation.surface: A virgin is advised to snog less often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' looks like kissing, which suits 'Virgin', but here it means to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgin snow is untouched and unmarked, so the word can mean perfectly clean, without a blemish.

clue.text: Bloody hell! Biden just started something else!

indicators.note: a thing barely begun has got no further than its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
something other is something else

explanation.surface: An exasperated onlooker swears as President Biden launches yet another initiative.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation definition is a mild British oath: 'Bother!' is said where an American might say 'darn'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are interjections of annoyance; 'bother!' is simply the milder, politer expletive of exasperation.

clue.text: Show willing, applying pressure to sex partner on testicle

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
slang for someone you sleep with
slang for a testicle

explanation.surface: A cruder picture: someone proves keen by pressing on a partner's private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces simply sit side by side in clue order; 'applying ... to' and 'on' only glue them.
explanation.definitionFit: To play ball is the idiom for cooperating, going along with what others want.

clue.text: Labour's second electoral triumph? Repeat that!

blocks.note: the second letter of the word
a seat won from a rival party at an election

explanation.surface: Someone hopes Labour can win a second election in a row and calls for an encore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a second term, but it picks the second letter of 'Labour'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouting 'Again!' is how you ask for something to be done once more, an encore request.

clue.text: Penny, stick politician in balls, quick!

indicators.note: to stick one thing somewhere is to push it into place
in places one piece inside the other, completing the instruction to insert

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for penny
balls means nonsense, rot
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: An urgent order to shove a politician somewhere painful, and fast.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'balls' means nonsense, not testicles. The insertion instruction is split around the politician: 'stick' before, 'in' after.
explanation.definitionFit: Prompt as an adjective means done without delay, so a synonym for speedy or immediate.

clue.text: Being realistic, sadly I'm crap at keeping good

definitions.note: a participial phrase standing for the adjective

indicators.note: something done sadly is done badly or wretchedly, so the letters end up in a poor state
to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A confession of mediocrity: being honest, I'm just bad at being good.
explanation.walkthrough: The self-deprecating 'I'm crap at' looks like the meaning of the clue, but it is just letters to shuffle around a G.
explanation.definitionFit: Pragmatic means dealing sensibly with things as they actually are, which is what a realistic person does.

clue.text: Well, work with Cyclops and one will get a poor view of things

blocks.note: both are exclamations of surprise
an op is a work, short for opus
Cyclops is the setter, who calls himself I
a means one

explanation.surface: Collaborate with a one-eyed giant and you'll end up seeing badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter's pseudonym, so the setter stands for I. OP (opus) is a numbered musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: Myopia is short-sightedness, where distant objects look blurred, literally a poor view of things.

clue.text: Progress, and benefit from oral sex, article concealed

indicators.note: something concealed is hidden away inside something else

blocks.note: to get is to receive or benefit from
the indefinite article
head is slang for oral sex

explanation.surface: A career tip: advance by enjoying sexual favours while hiding the evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is slang for oral sex. The article falls between the two words of the phrase, so the enumeration splits around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To get ahead is the idiom for advancing in life or career, making headway.

clue.text: Avoidance of booze – muscles can, as a consequence, start off

indicators.note: with its start taken off a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: abs are abdominal muscles
a tin is a can
hence means as a consequence; without its first letter

explanation.surface: Giving up drink means your muscles can get going again as a result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a consequence' is HENCE; 'start off' removes its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstinence is refraining from something, and in everyday use it most often means teetotalism, refusing alcohol.

clue.text: Supporters attending unfinished sequence of games eat here

definitions.note: a phrase describing a place, standing for the noun

indicators.note: something left unfinished lacks its ending, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: bras support the bust
a series is a run of matches; lose the last letter

explanation.surface: Fans following a half-played run of matches stop to grab a meal at this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' looks like sports fans, which suits the games, but they are undergarments. The definition is a description of the place: where you eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A brasserie is an informal French-style restaurant, a place where diners come for food.

clue.text: City backed Boris, doing a U-turn – arse!

indicators.note: going backwards means the letters run from right to left
a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the order flips

blocks.note: Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city
Boris Johnson was Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's financial backers watch him reverse a policy and curse him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' suggests the City of London's financiers, but it is the crossword's favourite ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Rump is the hindquarters or buttocks, so it is a synonym for the bottom.

clue.text: The bloke's stuck in stew pot

indicators.note: something stuck in something else is lodged inside it

blocks.note: a hash is a stew of chopped meat
belonging to the man

explanation.surface: A man is trapped inside a cooking pot full of stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' is the definition and slang for cannabis, not a cooking vessel; 'stew pot' reads as one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Pot is slang for cannabis, and hashish is the resin form of the same drug.

clue.text: Copper getting material on TV presenter

blocks.note: serge is a hard-wearing twill fabric
Ant McPartlin, of the British TV duo Ant and Dec

explanation.surface: A police officer digs up dirt on a television host.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant and Dec are a famous British presenting double act. In a down clue, 'on' puts the fabric above the presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: A copper is a police officer, and a sergeant is a particular police rank.

clue.text: Our old PM has cracked – about to resign?

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so its letters are rearranged
about means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to quit is to resign

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister has had a breakdown and may step down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has cracked' looks like a nervous collapse, but 'has' is the fodder. H. H. Asquith was Liberal Prime Minister from 1908 to 1916.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert Asquith led the British government early in the twentieth century, so he is a former premier.

clue.text: Tabloid, with no leader left, associates with rotten criminal

indicators.note: having no leader means the front letter is missing

blocks.note: the Sun, the British tabloid newspaper, minus its first letter
L is the abbreviation for left
rotten means very bad, awful

explanation.surface: A newspaper, its editor gone, keeps company with a corrupt crook.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid paper, beheaded here to UN.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminal as an adjective means against the law, which is exactly what unlawful means.

clue.text: Requirement in dating ad? Gosh – having a change of heart!

indicators.note: a change at the heart means the middle of the word is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written; its two central letters swap

explanation.surface: Someone reading lonely-hearts listings exclaims at what they ask for, then changes their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the inner pair of letters changes places. The answer is the personal-ad shorthand Good Sense Of Humour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lonely-hearts advertisements commonly ask for a good sense of humour, abbreviated in classifieds to save space.

clue.text: The woman's a big-mouthed, vacant, proclaiming type

indicators.note: a vacant thing is emptied, so only its outside letters remain

blocks.note: belonging to the woman
taken as written
big-mouthed means loud; emptied of its middle

explanation.surface: A woman is described as a loud, empty-headed person forever making announcements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacant' sounds like an insult about her mind, but it empties LOUD of its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A herald was an official messenger who made public announcements, a person who proclaims news.

clue.text: Peacekeepers supposedly manipulated oil price, too (sod all taken off)

indicators.note: something taken off is removed from the whole
something manipulated is worked into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then one O removed
sod all is British slang for nothing, zero, the letter O; this is what is removed

explanation.surface: A sneer at those who keep order, accused of rigging fuel prices and taking a cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one nothing (O) from OIL PRICE TOO, then rearrange the rest. 'Supposedly' is the setter's dig: these forces are meant to keep the peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Officers equipped to handle disorder are meant to restore calm, so they are nominally peacekeepers, hence the sceptical qualifier.

clue.text: Dense old bust mangled by brassiere, finally

indicators.note: something mangled is crushed out of shape, so its letters are rearranged
finally points to the very end of the word, its last letter

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written, to be rearranged
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: An ageing, heavy chest has been squashed out of shape by an ill-fitting bra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dense' seems to describe the bust, but it is the definition, meaning stupid.
explanation.definitionFit: Dense and obtuse are both adjectives for someone slow to understand, synonyms for dim-witted.

clue.text: Aggressive leader's installed

blocks.note: first meaning: the warmongering Russian president
second meaning: a two-word phrasal verb for placed in position, as a fitting is

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is PUT IN, two words run together, which the single enumeration hides.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian president invaded Ukraine, so he is a hostile ruler; and something installed has been placed in position.

clue.text: Salacious Rupert in trouble

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disarray, so its letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Rupert Murdoch's sleazy tabloid empire lands him in hot water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like part of 'in trouble' but it is fodder too; only 'trouble' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Prurient means having an excessive interest in sexual matters, close in sense to lewd or lecherous.

clue.text: It's cheap to have a go cuddling a wife and daughter

indicators.note: to cuddle is to wrap your arms round, so one piece embraces another

blocks.note: to try is to have a go
taken as written
W is the abbreviation for wife
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Groping both a man's wife and his daughter is a low move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a go' suggests making a pass, but it is just TRY, which goes round the other three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawdry means showy but of poor quality, so cheap in the sense of tacky and tasteless.

clue.text: Bluster from Republican with strange tan

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so the letters fall into an odd order

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Hot air from an orange-tinted Republican politician, an obvious dig at Donald Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd suntan points at Trump, but the pieces are a party abbreviation and three letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluster is loud, aggressive talk with little substance, much like a ranting tirade.

clue.text: Some remember lingerie which was once divided

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun

indicators.note: some of the text is only a part of it, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone fondly recalls a set of underwear that once came in two pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the city split by the Wall between 1961 and 1989.
explanation.definitionFit: The German capital was partitioned into East and West sectors during the Cold War, separated by the Wall.

clue.text: Tabloid stung and given a tanning

blocks.note: the Sun, the British tabloid newspaper
to get burnt is to be stung, cheated

explanation.surface: A newspaper is caught in a sting operation and then given a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid. 'Given a tanning' looks like a thrashing, but it means a skin burn from the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunburnt skin has been darkened and reddened by sunlight exposure, literally tanned by rays.
